prompt: Explain gerrymandering using only golf metaphors. Keep going after the metaphor files a complaint.
response:
Alright, let’s tee this up.

Gerrymandering is when someone redesigns a golf course—not to make it a fair test of skill—but to guarantee that one particular golfer wins the club championship, no matter how they actually play.

Imagine you’re the course designer, and you have the power to move tee boxes, shift fairways, redraw out-of-bounds lines, and relocate hazards. You’re not doing it for aesthetics or challenge. You’re doing it so that your buddy Dave, who has a brutal slice and can’t putt on fast greens, still wins the match play final.

Here’s how you do it.

---

**Packing the Rough**

You take all the opponents who can actually hit fairways and you funnel them onto the same nine-hole stretch. You narrow those fairways to the width of a welcome mat. You grow the rough to U.S. Open levels—thick, penal, wrist-breaking. You tuck the pins behind deep bunkers and on triple-breaking slopes. Every hole on that side becomes a survival test. The opponents beat each other up just trying to make bogey. They’re exhausted by the turn. Meanwhile, their scores relative to each other cancel out. One of them will advance, but they’ll be so bruised that Dave will have an easy time in the final.

That’s “packing.” You concentrate the competition’s strength into a few brutal holes so they knock each other out, wasting their good shots in the hay.

---

**Cracking the Field**

The opposite move: you take a few strong opponents and you scatter them across the entire course, isolating each one in a separate foursome full of Dave’s buddies. You give each of those foursomes its own special tees. For the strong player, you stretch the course to 7,800 yards, with forced carries over water, into the wind. For Dave’s buddies in the same group, you move their tees up to the ladies’ markers, let them roll the ball in the fairway, and give them gimmes inside the leather. The strong player shoots 74 under brutal conditions; Dave’s buddy shoots 72 with the setup help. The strong player misses the cut by one. You’ve “cracked” the field, splitting the opposition into small, diluted groups where the stacked conditions drown them one by one.

---

**The Moving Hole**

Now, the real artistry: you don’t just move the tees. You move the actual hole locations after the round has started. You see Dave is leaking oil on the back nine, so you radio the maintenance crew: “Make the 14th green stimp at 14 for the next group, but for Dave’s match, roll it and put the cup in a valley where everything funnels to the hole.” For the opponent, the same green becomes a lightning-fast dome where a missed four-footer rolls 20 feet away. You’re not changing the course, you’re just “adjusting the pin positions” to match the players. The rules official shrugs; it’s technically the same course. But one guy is playing mini-golf and the other is at Augusta on Sunday.

---

**The Handicap Mirage**

Here’s the sophisticated version. You maintain a perfectly legitimate handicap system, but you get to decide which rounds count for the index. Dave plays all his casual rounds on a par-3 executive course with no wind and perfect greens. Those scores establish his handicap. The challengers are required to post their scores from the 7,500-yard championship tees, in March, in a gale. When they meet for the club championship, the “handicap strokes” Dave gets are based on a fiction: that his easy-course 78 is equivalent to their storm-tossed 82. The strokes fall on the hardest holes. Dave essentially starts 2-up before he even hits a tee shot. The system looks fair on paper—everyone has a handicap—but the formula was rigged by controlling which data goes into it.

---

**The Unplayable Lie Rule**

Finally, you interpret the rulebook creatively. When an opponent hits a drive into the fairway, you declare that area a “newly seeded divot zone—ground under repair, free drop in the bunker.” When Dave pipes one into the trees, you discover an old local rule that “wooded areas left of the 7th are considered lateral hazards, drop with one-stroke penalty but clear shot to the green.” You’re not breaking the rules; you’re the one writing the local rules sheet the night before the tournament. You’ve effectively gerrymandered the course’s boundaries so that Dave’s misses are minor inconveniences, and his opponents’ perfect shots land in jail.

---

In short, gerrymandering is designing the golf course, the tee boxes, the pin positions, the handicaps, and the local rules so that Dave—who slices, can’t putt, and whines about the wind—wins the club championship, again and again, without ever having to beat the field straight up. The course looks beautiful from the clubhouse balcony. The scorecard seems normal. But every contour, every hazard, every blade of grass has been bent toward a predetermined result.

And when the losers complain, you say, “Hey, we all played the same 18 holes.” Technically true. But you know, and they know, that the course was rigged before the first tee shot was ever struck.
